messages.author: 05a98452bfc1172d
messages.subject: "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts: I sometimes get Rhat values of "nan" when using PyStan. This happens for certain data sets repeatedly. I think I get these values for variables that are actually very close to zero and seem well converged based on the effective sample size (n_eff) values. Is this a bug in stan?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
If R-hat is NaN and n_eff is not NaN, it's almost certainly
a precision problemin the arithmetic.

Could you send us a model and data set for which it happens so
we can diagnose?

There may be loss of arithmetic precision in R-hat compared to
what we could do ideally. The problem is that floating point
subtraction of values close to each other results in so-called
catastrophic cancellation, losing an arbitrary amount of precision.
Something like Welford's algorithm is required to maintain stability
for sample variance calculations, and I'm not sure how PyStan has implemented
R-hat.

For example, this model is problematic arithmetically:

fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(1,1e-20); }")

and produces

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y 1 0.0 0 1 1 1 1 1 4000 Inf
lp__ -15407440 422002.9 26689805 -61629758 -15407440 0 0 0 4000 1.500106e+14


There's really nothing we can do about such models numerically. What
you have to do from a user perspective is use a parameterizations

z = y - 1,

which can be handled stably because you can represent numbers close to zero well.

parameters { real z; } model { z ~ normal(0,1e-20); }

The problem is that there's still no way to represent y = z + 1, but
you can get close to log(y) by using

log_y <- log1p(z);

We're gradually pulling all these implementations back into
the core Stan C++ code, so at least we'll only have one fix to make
for issues like this in the near future.

- Bob

P.S. I'm going to drop the above discussion into a new section on
arithmetic in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
or maybe an entire chapter on arithmetic stability of various operators.

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
Hi Jesse,

Yes, this is an issue. While R will let you divide by zero (or nearly
zero) quickly and without any problem (other than throwing up an 'Inf'),
Python raises an exception. The current way PyStan handles this probably
isn't the best. If you have a simple case where nan isn't appropriate,
would you mind opening an issue on PyStan's github site?

On the other hand, if there really is zero variance among the chains
with respect to some parameter, rhat and n_eff should be 'nan'.

Thanks,

-a

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
Are you using double-precision floating point? As far as I
know, R's just using standard IEEE floating point.

The usual problems are with subtraction, not division, unless
you get so close to zero that the division overflows to +inf.
But if that happens for two numbers, it should happen in R, too.

And then once you get inf, everything is inf or NaN. You can't
divide inf/inf or subract (inf - inf), although you can add (inf + inf)
and get inf as long as the infs are the right sign.

- Bob

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
Hi Bob,

Yeah, Python throws an error we have to catch:

> In [4]: 1 / 1e-500
> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ZeroDivisionError Traceback (most recent call last)
> <ipython-input-4-ba7ce1d0dee4> in <module>()
> ----> 1 1 / 1e-500
>
> ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero

rhat and n_eff are bottlenecks on huge models so there's been a lot of
churn trying to get it right AND fast. Originally I had everything going
through Stan and C++ but handing things off to C++ and then handing it
back to Python was too inefficient. If Stan could expose some way for
RStan and PyStan to calculate rhat and n_eff, that would be fantastic.
Right now I believe there are 3 implementations of the rhat and n_eff
calculations (one for each language).

I'd definitely welcome help on this, if anyone is interested.

Thanks,

-a

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
Dear Paula,

PyStan's rhat calculation has some bugs associated with it. In the
future, PyStan will use the same rhat code as CmdStan uses.

There are known issues when the variance of the parameter is zero but it
sounds like that's not what's happening here. If you can reproduce the
problem with model code and data you're willing to share, I can look
into it. If that's not possible, I'd suggest trying to run the model in
RStan and seeing if rhat is displayed.

Best,

Allen

parts:
Dear Allen, 

I appreciate your help, thank you!
Please find attached the data and the model. 

Here's a quick description of the model:
I want to fit the data points with a line. The data has measurement errors. So xerr and yerr is simply the uncertainties on the parameters.

Cheers!
Paula

On Mon, Sep 21, 2015 at 10:26 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
Dear Paula,

PyStan's rhat calculation has some bugs associated with it. In the
future, PyStan will use the same rhat code as CmdStan uses.

There are known issues when the variance of the parameter is zero but it
sounds like that's not what's happening here. If you can reproduce the
problem with model code and data you're willing to share, I can look
into it.  If that's not possible, I'd suggest trying to run the model in
RStan and seeing if rhat is displayed.

Best,

Allen


On 09/21, Paula Sarkis wrote:
> I have around 100 parameters. All the parameters have n_eff = 6668 and Rhat
> = 1.0 except for only 1 parameter (the most important one). This parameter
> has n_eff = 6668 but Rhat = nan
>
> I am running MCMC with 10,000 iterations, warmup = 5,000 and with 4 chains.
> So that's a total of 20,000 draws. n_eff of lp is 3938 and Rhat = 1.0.
>
> Any idea why I am getting Rhat  = nan?
>
> On Mon, Sep 21, 2015 at 7:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > The manual provides the formula in the MCMC chapter.
> >
> > I don't know that there's a way for R-hat to be NaN without
> > n_eff being NaN.
> >
> > If PyStan lets you dump the output in the CSV format which
> > CmdStan can read, you could check that way.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Sep 21, 2015, at 12:00 PM, Paula Sarkis <paula.s...@gmail.com>
> > wrote:
> > >
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I am having the same problem. The trace plot looks perfect however the
> > value of Rhat is nan.
> > >
> > > Can you please give me some details on how to evaluate n_eff for each
> > parameter. Also, how to evaluate lp. I've been having the 'nan' problem
> > with rhat many times now, I want to double check whether my model is ill
> > defined or if the problem is from python.
> > >
> > > Cheers,
> > > Paula
> > >
> > > On Thursday, December 18, 2014 at 5:55:24 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > If R-hat is NaN and n_eff is not NaN, it's almost certainly
> > > a precision problemin the arithmetic.
> > >
> > > Could you send us a model and data set for which it happens so
> > > we can diagnose?
> > >
> > > There may be loss of arithmetic precision in R-hat compared to
> > > what we could do ideally.  The problem is that floating point
> > > subtraction of values close to each other results in so-called
> > > catastrophic cancellation, losing an arbitrary amount of precision.
> > > Something like Welford's algorithm is required to maintain stability
> > > for sample variance calculations, and I'm not sure how PyStan has
> > implemented
> > > R-hat.
> > >
> > > For example, this model is problematic arithmetically:
> > >
> > > fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~
> > normal(1,1e-20); }")
> > >
> > > and produces
> > >
> > >           mean  se_mean       sd      2.5%       25% 50% 75% 97.5%
> > n_eff         Rhat
> > > y            1      0.0        0         1         1   1   1     1
> > 4000          Inf
> > > lp__ -15407440 422002.9 26689805 -61629758 -15407440   0   0     0  4000
> > 1.500106e+14
> > >
> > >
> > > There's really nothing we can do about such models numerically.  What
> > > you have to do from a user perspective is use a parameterizations
> > >
> > >   z = y - 1,
> > >
> > > which can be handled stably because you can represent numbers close to
> > zero well.
> > >
> > > parameters { real z; } model { z ~ normal(0,1e-20); }
> > >
> > > The problem is that there's still no way to represent y = z + 1, but
> > > you can get close to log(y) by using
> > >
> > >   log_y <- log1p(z);
> > >
> > > We're gradually pulling all these implementations back into
> > > the core Stan C++ code, so at least we'll only have one fix to make
> > > for issues like this in the near future.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > P.S.  I'm going to drop the above discussion into a new section on
> > >       arithmetic in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
> > >       or maybe an entire chapter on arithmetic stability of various
> > operators.

I am also having this issue for some of my parameters in PyStan. Rhat = nan, but n_eff=iterations. My model code is:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# model predicting weight and height from waist size and shoe size.
# fake data
N = 100 # number per group

height_m = np.random.normal(5.7, 0.3, N)
shoe_size_m = height_m * 3.5 + np.random.normal(0,0.5,N) - 10
weight_m = height_m ** 2.8 + (np.random.gamma(3,2,N) - 2 ** 2) * 18
waist_size_m = weight_m ** 0.33 * height_m + 4 + np.random.normal(0,0.5,N)
is_male_m = np.ones(N)
# women
height_w = np.random.normal(5.2, 0.3, N)
shoe_size_w = height_w * 3.4 + np.random.normal(0,0.5,N) - 10
weight_w = height_w ** 2.8 + (np.random.gamma(3,2,N) - 2 ** 2) * 10 + 20
waist_size_w = weight_w ** 0.33 * height_w + np.random.normal(0,0.7,N)
is_male_w = np.ones(N) + 1

height = np.append(height_m, height_w)
shoe_size = np.append(shoe_size_m, shoe_size_w)
weight = np.append(weight_m, weight_w)
waist_size = np.append(waist_size_m, waist_size_w)
group = np.append(is_male_m, is_male_w).astype(int)

y = np.matrix([list(height), list(np.log(weight))]).T
x = np.matrix([list(waist_size), list(shoe_size)]).T

             'J': np.shape(x)[1],

      cholesky_factor_corr[L] omega_u;
      vector<lower=0>[K] sigma; // population standard deviation
      vector[L] u; // random intercepts
      vector<lower=0>[L] sigma_u; // random intercepts SD
    }
    model {
      vector[K] mu[N];
      matrix[K,K] Sigma;
      matrix[L,L] Sigma_u;
      vector[L] zeros;
      
      Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma, omega);
      Sigma_u <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, omega_u);
      
      for (l in 1:L)
        zeros[l] <- 0;
      
      u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zeros, Sigma_u);
        
      for (n in 1:N)
        mu[n] <- beta * x[n] + intercept + u[random[N]];
        
      // Priors
      to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 5);
      omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      omega_u ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
      sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
      sigma_u ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
      
      // Data Model
      y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, Sigma);
    }
    """

fit = pystan.stan(model_code=model_code, data=model_dat,
                  iter=1000, chains=2,

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "nan" values for Rhat in pystan
parts:
They're not margins in the sense that they're deterministic.
I just figured it'd be easier to scan that way, but it's
definitely wasteful.

Right now, the problem in printing is that there are two
ways things can have the same value in every draw. One is
to be a discrete generated quantity that never changes. This
can happen in event probability calculations if the probability
is very close to 0 or 1 or the chains aren't run for many
iterations (you need many more iterations to estimate tail
probabilities well).

So I don't know if there's a good way to tell the ones that
are constant by design (diagonal of a correlation matrix) and
ones that are random quantities, but constant in a chain
because every draw has produced the same value.

- Bob
